drivingQuestion: What distinguishes the mishna's first clause (no dispute) from its latter clause (dispute)?
outcomeNote: The school of R' Yannai's answer is refined into a doubt-based distinction

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא דְּלָא פְּלִיגִי, וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא דִּפְלִיגִי?
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara asks: «What is different» in the «first clause» of the mishna, when she inherited property before she was betrothed, such «that» Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel «do not disagree, and what is different» in «the latter clause,» when she inherited property after betrothal, such «that they disagree?» If the dispute concerns the right to her property after she is betrothed, what difference does it make whether her ownership began before or after the betrothal?

segments.he: אָמְרִי דְּבֵי רַבִּי יַנַּאי: רֵישָׁא — בִּזְכוּתָהּ נָפְלוּ. סֵיפָא — בִּזְכוּתוֹ נָפְלוּ.
segments.en: The Gemara answers that the Sages «of the school of Rabbi Yannai say: In the first clause,» where she inherited the property before her betrothal, the inheritance «was bequeathed» to her during a period when «she» had «rights» to her property, whereas «in the latter clause,» the inheritance «was bequeathed» to her during a period when «he» had «rights» to her property.

segments.he: אִם בִּזְכוּתוֹ נָפְלוּ, כִּי מָכְרָה וְנָתְנָה אַמַּאי קַיָּים? אֶלָּא: רֵישָׁא — וַדַּאי בִּזְכוּתָהּ נָפְלוּ. סֵיפָא — אֵימַר בִּזְכוּתָהּ, אֵימַר בִּזְכוּתוֹ. לְכַתְּחִלָּה לֹא תִּמְכּוֹר, אִם מָכְרָה וְנָתְנָה — קַיָּים.
segments.en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: «If,» in the latter clause the property «was bequeathed» to her when «he» had «rights» to it, «why» is the transaction «valid when she sold» it «or gave» it away? «Rather,» in «the first clause,» where she inherited the property before her betrothal, it «certainly was bequeathed» to her when «she» had «rights» to it and it therefore fully belongs to her. However, in «the latter clause,» where she inherited it after her betrothal, one can «say» that perhaps during this time «she has rights» to it, or «say» that perhaps during this time «he has rights» to it. Since the ownership of the property is a matter of uncertainty, Beit Hillel rule that «she may not sell ab initio,» but «if she sold» it «or gave» it away, the transaction is «valid.»

moves.summary: why agreement in the first clause and dispute in the latter?
moves.about: why BS and BH agree when property fell before betrothal but dispute when it fell after
before betrothal the property fell under her rights, after betrothal under his

moves.summary: then why is her sale valid?
moves.about: if the property fell under the husband's rights, her sale should not be valid

moves.summary: latter clause is a doubt: not ab initio, valid after the fact
moves.about: BH's 'she may not sell' rests on doubt whose rights the property fell under, so a sale after the fact stands
